title: Multiscale Characterization of Dislocation Cell Structures in LPBF Processed 316L Stainless Steels
content: Metal-based Additive Manufacturing (MAM) techniques such as Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is an emerging manufacturing process used to fabricate metallic parts with complex geometries. In the LPBF process, a uniform layer of metallic powder is spread over a powder bed and is then selectively melted by the application of a laser beam. The repetitive melting and cooling of the process on the addition of layers leads to the formation of a solidified net-shaped 3D part. The additive nature of LPBF allows complex parts to be manufactured in net-shape, with less waste, and reduced processing time. The LPBF process has been used for rapid prototyping and small batch processing of complex parts for aerospace, automotive, and biomedical applications [1]. The AM fabrication results in parts with hierarchical microstructures and metastable phases that provide superior mechanical properties to traditionally manufactured parts [2]. The LPBF process parameters strongly influence the microstructure and subsequent mechanical properties of the materials as they dictate the spatio-temporal variations in the thermal history of the part [3]. LPBF process conditions result in steep thermal gradients (∼106 K/m) and rapid cooling rates (∼105 – 106 K/s), these non-equilibrium conditions during LPBF typically result in long columnar grains with meta-stable phases. The thermal history also dictates the distribution of defects found inside the part such as porosity, keyhole defects, ‘lack of fusion’ defects, spatter, and inclusions [2]. The non-uniform distribution of flaws yields inconsistent mechanical properties, which is a barrier to qualify these parts using standard ‘process-centric’ qualification and certification processes, used for traditionally manufactured safety-critical parts [4]. Therefore, the development of a new ‘microstructure-centric’ qualification framework for the rapid qualification of AM components is needed [5]. This new framework necessitates a comprehensive understanding of how the processing conditions can be used to control the microstructure of parts resulting in consistent part performance vis-à-vis a well-curated process-structure-property dataset.
